input.question: How is it possible that everything falls at the same speed regardless of mass? Is there a limit where this approximation stops to be correct?
input.ground_truth: > Is there a limit where this approximation stops to be correct? Yes. The "limit of the approximation" is that the mass of the thing dropped is negligible compared to the mass of the Earth. Consider two masses M1 and M2 at a distance R. The gravitational force F between them will be G\*M1\*M2/R^2 , so the acceleration of the first object will be F/M1 = G\*M2/R^2 and the acceleration of the second object will be F/M2 = G\*M1/R^2 The two objects will thus accelerate towards each other at a rate of G\*(M1 + M2)/R^2 . In the case of a feather or hammer on the Earth, M1 is so much larger than M2 that the effects of M2 can be ignored. In this case, both hammer and feather would have the same acceleration.

response.prediction:
Alright, let’s imagine you have a feather and a rock. If you drop them at the same time, they both hit the ground at the same time if there is no air (like on the moon!). This happens because, on Earth, the air can make the feather fall more slowly, but if we ignore the air, both fall at the same speed.

Now, why do they fall at the same speed? Well, the Earth pulls on everything with gravity, but a heavy thing (like a rock) is harder to move than a light thing (like a feather). However, gravity also pulls harder on the heavy thing. These two things balance out, so everything falls at the same speed if there’s no air.

But wait! This is only true if we don’t go too high or too fast. If you drop something from really, really high (like from a tall mountain to space), or if you go super fast, then other things start to matter, and they don’t fall exactly the same speed anymore. But for most things we drop every day, they all fall at the same speed.

So, the rule works very well for normal stuff, but if things get really big or really fast, we need to think a little harder!
